subtitle: What it is, and how to do it

scenes.narration: Scidonia Limited presents Vericoding: an introduction in six parts.

visual.title: Vericoding
visual.subtitle: Programs, specifications and proofs, in one language

scenes.narration: Vericoding is a way of writing software where the specification, the proof, and the program are all one artefact, checked by a machine.

visual.heading: Tests sample. Proofs quantify.

left.title: A test suite
left.caption: a handful of inputs, observed once

right.title: A specification
right.caption: a claim about every input, proved

conclusion.text: The proof is the certificate for the whole region.

scenes.narration: Normally we test. A test runs the program on a handful of inputs, and we hope the rest behave. A specification is different. It says something about every possible input, and a proof is a certificate that the code meets it. Tests sample. Proofs quantify.

visual.heading: One artefact, three obligations

result.label: One language
result.detail: the specification cannot drift away from the implementation

scenes.narration: So a vericoded program is three things at once. The code. A statement of what that code must mean. And a proof, machine-checked step by step, that the code meets the statement. One language for all three, so the specification cannot drift away from the implementation.

visual.heading: Proof engineering was the bottleneck

points.text: Writing the proofs took specialists, for far longer than writing the code
Large language models changed the economics
Routine goals discharged · lemmas suggested · broken proofs repaired

emphasis.text: The proof is no longer the expensive part.

scenes.narration: Why now? Proving used to be the bottleneck. A theorem prover could check everything, but writing the proofs took specialists far longer than writing the code. Large language models changed the economics. Routine obligations get discharged, lemmas get suggested, broken proofs get repaired. The proof is no longer the expensive part.

visual.heading: Iterate on intent, not operation

left.title: Without vericoding
lines: change the code, hope the meaning survived
each feature widens the surface you cannot check

right.title: With vericoding
lines: change the specification, see what breaks

visual.note: The conversation moves to what the program must mean.

scenes.narration: That moves the scarce resource. The machine cannot invent what your program must mean. You iterate at the specification surface, in conversation, and the implementation becomes something you can replace later. The dialectic is about intent, not operation.
Next, why a proof is, literally, a program.

visual.title: Proofs are programs
visual.subtitle: Why a proof assistant and a compiler are the same machine

scenes.narration: A theorem prover is a program for authoring and checking proofs. And since proofs can be seen as programs, the prover can be thought of as a programming language environment.

visual.heading: A claim, a proof, and a checker that cannot be argued with

stages.label: Proof
stages.detail: a term that should inhabit it

visual.note: Keeping the kernel small is what makes it worth trusting.

scenes.narration: You state a claim, you give a proof, and a small trusted program — the kernel — verifies every step. Nothing is taken on authority. A proof is a certificate: the checker accepts it, or it does not. Keeping the kernel small is what makes it worth trusting.

visual.heading: Propositions are types

rows.right: a witness and a proof about it

scenes.narration: The reason this can be a programming language is a correspondence. A proposition is a type, and a proof is a program of that type. Implication is a function. Conjunction is a pair. Disjunction is a tagged union. For all is a dependent function, and there exists is a witness paired with a proof about it.

visual.heading: A type that talks about a value
visual.code:
inductive Vec (α : Type) : Nat → Type where
  | nil : Vec α 0
  | cons (x : α) {n : Nat} : Vec α n → Vec α (n + 1)

-- There is no case for the empty vector:
-- it cannot have this type.
def head {α : Type} {n : Nat} (v : Vec α (n + 1)) : α :=
  match v with
  | .cons x _ => x

caption.text: An empty vector cannot be passed here. That is a type error, not an exception.

scenes.narration: That gives types which talk about values. Here is a vector: a list whose type records its length. The head of a non-empty vector has no empty case to handle, because an empty vector cannot have that type. Calling it on nothing is a type error, not an exception.

visual.heading: Checking a proof is type-checking a program

result.label: One machine
result.detail: one language carries the program, its specification, and its proof

scenes.narration: So checking a proof is type-checking a program. The proof assistant and the compiler are the same machine. That is what lets one language carry the program, the specification, and the proof.
Now, a first contract.

visual.title: Your first contract
visual.subtitle: A program, a statement about it, and a checked proof

scenes.narration: A contract is a theorem about a definition. Here is the smallest one worth writing.

visual.heading: The program
visual.code:
def maxOf (a b : Nat) : Nat :=
  if a ≤ b then b else a

caption.text: Correct, but nothing in this definition says what it means.

scenes.narration: Here is a very small program. maxOf returns the larger of two natural numbers. It is correct, but nothing about it says so.

visual.heading: The specification
visual.code:
def maxOf (a b : Nat) : Nat :=
  if a ≤ b then b else a

theorem le_maxOf_left (a b : Nat) : a ≤ maxOf a b := by
  sorry

caption.text: A statement about every pair of numbers, not a sample. The proof replaces sorry.

scenes.narration: The specification is another term in the same language. For all a and b, a is at most maxOf a b. That is a statement about every pair of numbers, not a sample.

visual.heading: The proof, and the goal state Lean prints
visual.code:
def maxOf (a b : Nat) : Nat :=
  if a ≤ b then b else a

theorem le_maxOf_left (a b : Nat) : a ≤ maxOf a b := by
  unfold maxOf
  split
  · rename_i h
    omega
  · omega

goals.label: after split
goals.text:
case isTrue
a b : Nat
h : a ≤ b
⊢ a ≤ b

caption.text: Every step is checked by the kernel. The goal text above is Lean's, not ours.

scenes.narration: The proof is a program of that statement's type. We unfold the definition, split on the comparison, and in each branch the arithmetic closes the goal. Lean prints the goal state after every step, so the proof is not a story about the code; it is the machine's own working.

visual.heading: Two kinds of error

cards.title: Error of reasoning
cards.body: The steps do not follow. The kernel rejects them, and there is nothing to argue with.

cards.title: Error of interpretation
cards.body: The specification says the wrong thing. It is written down, in the same language, so it can be read and revised.

visual.note: Without a specification, both errors are silent.

scenes.narration: Two kinds of error now become visible. An error of reasoning, connecting things wrongly, is rejected: the kernel will not accept the step. An error of interpretation, misunderstanding what the code means, leaves an artefact. The specification you wrote is there to be read, and iterated on.
The proof is checked, not reviewed. Next, two ways to specify.

visual.title: Two ways to specify
visual.subtitle: Intrinsic or extrinsic, deep or shallow

scenes.narration: There are two ways to attach a claim to code, and two ways to embed a language in a prover. Both distinctions matter.

visual.heading: Intrinsic: the claim is in the type
visual.code:
def headOf (xs : List Nat) (h : xs ≠ []) : Nat :=
  match xs with
  | [] => absurd rfl h
  | x :: _ => x

caption.text: The empty case is present only to discharge the impossible hypothesis.

scenes.narration: Intrinsic specification puts the claim in the type. Here the caller supplies evidence that the list is not empty, so the function has no empty case. Illegal states become unrepresentable, and every caller gets the guarantee for free. The cost is that types get heavier, and evidence gets threaded through signatures.

visual.heading: Extrinsic: the claim is a theorem about it
visual.code:
def double (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n

theorem double_eq (n : Nat) : double n = 2 * n := by
  simp [double, Nat.two_mul]

caption.text: The program stays idiomatic; the specification grows by accretion.

scenes.narration: Extrinsic specification writes the plain program, then states a separate theorem about it. double is just addition, and the theorem says it equals two times its argument. The program stays idiomatic, and the specification can grow by accretion. The cost is that you have to find the right theorems.

visual.heading: A rule of thumb

right.title: Extrinsic · behaviour
lines: what a file contains after a write

scenes.narration: A rule of thumb. Use intrinsic specification for shape: lengths, non-emptiness, invariants of a data structure. Use extrinsic specification for behaviour: what a sort returns, what a file contains after a write, what a protocol did.

visual.heading: The second axis: what is inside the prover?

left.title: Deep embedding
lines: a semantics, then a theory about it
Iris for concurrency and unsafe code

right.title: What it buys, and costs
lines: the embedding and its theory are yours to trust
getting back to running code is a separate step

visual.note: Power is bought with a trusted model.

scenes.narration: There is a second axis. A deep embedding makes the language under study into data inside the prover, with a semantics and a theory built about it. Iris does this for concurrent and unsafe programs; interaction trees do it for effects. It buys reusable reasoning about hard semantics, and it costs you the embedding and its theory.

visual.heading: Shallow: the prover is the programming language

items.label: Proof
items.detail: a term checked by the same kernel

result.label: No gap
result.detail: the code you reason about is the code that runs

scenes.narration: A shallow embedding does not model the language; it uses it. The prover is the programming language. Terms are programs, types are specifications, and proofs are terms checked by the same kernel. There is no gap between the code you reason about and the code that runs.
This tutorial takes the shallow path. Next, what happens to the proofs when the code compiles.

visual.title: From proof to binary
visual.subtitle: Erasure, compilation, and the staircase of levels

scenes.narration: A proof is a static claim. What comes out of the compiler is a program with no prover in it.

visual.heading: What survives compilation

scenes.narration: Compilation erases whatever exists only for the proof. Proofs are propositions, and propositions carry no runtime data. What is left is the algorithm and its data. The guarantees are static, so nothing is re-checked at runtime, and the cost of having them is zero.

visual.heading: Lean compiles like a systems language
visual.note: Reference counting: deterministic destruction, no stop-the-world pause, in-place update when uniquely owned.
visual.afterword: Uniquely owned values are updated in place.

scenes.narration: Lean elaborates to its own intermediate representation, emits C, and links a small runtime into a native binary. Memory is managed by reference counting rather than a tracing collector, so destruction is deterministic, and a uniquely owned value can be updated in place.

visual.heading: Verification does not pay at runtime

points.text: The extracted sort compiled to a 3.4 MB binary
Byte-identical output to the interpreted run

emphasis.text: A measurement of this program, not a claim that verification makes code faster.

scenes.narration: In this tutorial's own measurement, the extracted sort compiled to a small binary, produced byte-identical output, and ran about twenty-seven times faster than interpreting the same file.

visual.heading: One program, many representations

proposed.text: Proposed architecture · not a settled result

scenes.narration: Zoom out, and the whole design is a staircase. Within a level you optimise: rewrite the program, keep its behaviour. Between levels you lower: a source language becomes a simpler one, and eventually machine code. Every vertical edge carries a refinement proof. This stack is a proposed architecture, not a settled result.
Next, what a verified program still has to assume about the world.

visual.title: Building the world
visual.subtitle: Effects, libraries, theories, and the bottom of the stack

scenes.narration: A verified program still has to talk to a world nobody verified. The question is what it is allowed to assume.

visual.heading: Effects are in the type

caption.text: The signature says the function can print. Nothing is hidden.

scenes.narration: Effects do not disappear. They become explicit. IO is a type, and a function that prints says so in its signature. Pure-looking code can still run at imperative speed: an array is a value in the type system and a mutable buffer in the implementation, updated in place when it is uniquely owned.

visual.heading: A binding is not a theory

left.title: A binding
lines: how to call the operating system
a few lines, and it compiles
nothing yet says what it means

right.title: A theory
lines: what a read returns, what a write leaves behind

visual.note: Contracts are written against the meaning.

scenes.narration: Real programs need the world: files, sockets, databases, time. Lean can call almost anything, so a binding is a few lines. But a binding is not a library you can verify against. A binding says how to call. A theory says what the call means, and contracts are written against the meaning.

visual.heading: Every theory ends in an assertion
visual.note: The bottom is exactly what you assume.

scenes.narration: Every theory ends in an assertion. The operating system, the network card, the database, are not vericoded. So the bottom of the stack is exactly what you assume. Keep the assumption small, explicit, and testable: differential testing against the real system, property-based checks, fuzzing at the boundary.

visual.heading: Much of the world is still unwritten

cards.title: LeanIn
cards.body: A high-performance concurrency runtime whose scheduling model is proved, and whose runtime is checked against it.

cards.title: JSON
cards.body: A complete implementation already ships with Lean.

cards.title: Databases
cards.body: A theory of transactions and isolation would let contracts speak about both.

visual.note: Files, text and time still need the same treatment. Vericoding is only in its infancy.

scenes.narration: Some of these theories exist, and many do not. LeanIn is one example: a concurrency runtime whose scheduling model is proved, and whose runtime is checked against that model. JSON already has a complete implementation in Lean. A theory of databases would let contracts speak about transactions and isolation. Files, text and time still have to be made precise in the same way. Vericoding is only in its infancy, and many important parts are still to be written.

visual.text: Write the specification. Let the proof be checked.

scenes.narration: Vericoding moves the work to the surface where a machine can check it: what the program must mean. Write the specification. Let the proof be checked.
